questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that developing a hybrid loop directly against real quantum hardware (Mistake 1) is expensive, not just risky?
options: Cloud providers refuse to allow development workloads on real hardware
A buggy loop run dozens of times during development, at real-hardware prices like the ~$77,265 example from Lesson 2, racks up large costs for runs that were never going to produce a usable result
Simulators are always less accurate than real hardware, so this isn't actually a mistake
Real hardware is technically incapable of running a loop more than once
questions.explain: The expense comes from running an unfinished, buggy loop repeatedly at real-hardware prices during development -- exactly the cost scale shown in Lesson 2's VQE example -- rather than developing against a free/near-free simulator first.

questions.q: What is the specific fix the lesson proposes for Mistake 3 (no cost ceiling on the optimization loop)?
options: Track cumulative spend inside the loop itself and halt with an alert if spend crosses a pre-set ceiling, independent of the max-iteration cap
Only run the loop on weekends when cloud pricing is lower
Disable all cost tracking since it adds overhead to the loop
Remove the max-iteration cap entirely so the loop always converges
questions.explain: An iteration cap alone doesn't protect against a loop that oscillates or plateaus without converging -- a real-time cumulative-spend check with its own ceiling is needed as an independent safeguard.

questions.q: The lesson states that at 1,000 shots, relative standard error is around 0.032. What practical mistake does ignoring this lead to (Mistake 4)?
options: Being unable to compute an expectation value at all without knowing the standard error
Concluding that two results which differ by less than a few standard errors represent a real, meaningful difference, when the difference may just be shot noise
Running too many shots and wasting money unnecessarily
Submitting circuits to the wrong quantum backend
questions.explain: Standard error quantifies the statistical uncertainty in a measured expectation value; a difference smaller than a few standard errors is statistically indistinguishable from noise, not evidence that one circuit or parameter set is genuinely better.

questions.q: What is the recommended fix for Mistake 5 (tight coupling to one provider's SDK)?
options: Write all orchestration logic inside the quantum circuit itself to avoid the need for an SDK

Define a thin internal interface (submit_circuit, get_result, estimate_cost) with provider-specific adapters behind it, so the orchestration code isn't rewritten when adding a backend or reacting to a pricing change
Avoid using any cloud quantum provider's SDK at all, even for the adapter layer
Always use exactly one provider for the lifetime of the project, since switching is never necessary
questions.explain: A thin internal interface with provider-specific adapters behind it is standard dependency-inversion applied to this domain -- it isolates the orchestration code from any single SDK's specifics, making it far cheaper to add or switch providers later.

questions.q: What is the lesson's core point in observing that none of the five common mistakes involve the quantum circuit itself being logically wrong?
options: Quantum circuits are never the source of any bugs in a hybrid system

The production engineering discipline needed for hybrid systems (test environments, retries, budget guards, statistical rigor, decoupling) is largely the same discipline used in any classical backend system, applied carefully to this domain
These mistakes are unique to quantum computing and have no classical software analog
Classical code quality doesn't actually matter for hybrid quantum projects
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames all five mistakes as ones a backend engineer would recognize in any non-quantum microservice -- reinforcing the course's overall framing that most of the engineering risk and skill in hybrid systems is classical, not quantum-specific.
